title: Data Ingestion: Files, COPY INTO & Auto Loader
subtitle: spark.read, schemas, COPY INTO, Auto Loader, checkpoints, schema evolution, rescued data — and debugging every ingestion incident
mantra: Land files faithfully and exactly once: the reader needs a grammar (schema), the loader needs a memory (COPY INTO tracking or a checkpoint), and business duplicates are Silver's job.
objectives: You can read CSV, JSON and Parquet with spark.read, set the right parsing options and choose explicit schema (StructType or DDL) over inference for production.
You can explain why re-running spark.read duplicates data and how COPY INTO's file tracking makes loads retryable and idempotent — including the 'changed file is still skipped' subtlety.
You can write COPY INTO with FILEFORMAT, FORMAT_OPTIONS, COPY_OPTIONS, PATTERN, FILES, VALIDATE and a SELECT transformation, and tell the two mergeSchema options apart.
You can write a production Auto Loader Bronze stream (cloudFiles, schemaLocation, checkpointLocation, toTable, availableNow) and explain schemaLocation vs checkpointLocation.
You can predict Auto Loader's schema inference (strings by default, 50 GB / 1000-file sample, hints, inferColumnTypes), schema evolution modes and rescued data.
You can explain why file-level exactly-once does not prevent duplicate business keys, and where dedup/MERGE belongs.
You can choose between spark.read, COPY INTO and Auto Loader and answer the classic exam traps.
You can debug missing rows, overwritten files, schema shifts, missing columns, duplicate IDs, malformed CSV and checkpoint incidents with an ordered checklist.

sections.title: Ingestion: The Problem & the Ladder
sections.hook: Almost every pipeline starts with files you didn't write — this chapter is how you land them safely, once.

blocks.text: **Ingestion** is the process by which data that lives *outside* your target platform is brought *into* it — e.g. into a Delta table governed by Unity Catalog.

External system
   ├── CSV files
   ├── JSON
   ├── Parquet
   ├── API export          ──►  ingestion  ──►  Delta table
   ├── Kafka                                    (Databricks)
   ├── Database
   └── object storage
blocks.caption: Many sources, one goal: a reliable Delta table

blocks.text: This chapter (Phase 4) focuses on **file-based ingestion**: data that arrives as files in cloud storage or a Unity Catalog Volume.
**Running example.** An e-shop's operational system writes a new JSON file every **5 minutes** into `s3://company/orders/` — `orders_2026_09_28_0001.json`, `…_0002.json`, `…_0003.json` …

blocks.caption: Where the files must end up

blocks.text: The first problem is deceptively simple: **how do I read these files — and only the ones I haven't read yet?**

data lives somewhere
        ↓
 I must DISCOVER it
        ↓
 I must READ it
        ↓
 I must INTERPRET it with a schema
        ↓
 I must REMEMBER what I already processed
        ↓
 I must WRITE it reliably to Delta
blocks.caption: The six questions every ingestion pipeline answers

blocks.text:
FILES → spark.read → schema → batch ingestion
       → COPY INTO → Auto Loader → incremental discovery
       → checkpoint + schemaLocation → schema evolution
       → rescued data → production debugging
blocks.caption: The ladder of this chapter: lowest abstraction first

blocks.title: Recap: you've met the outlines before
blocks.text: Chapter 2 introduced batch vs incremental, checkpoints, schema enforcement/evolution and the medallion layers; Chapter 10 previewed Phase 4. Here every one of those ideas gets its real syntax, its failure modes and its debugging checklist.

blocks.label: Think first: the orders folder gains 288 files a day. Name three things your loader must decide or remember.
blocks.text: (1) **Which files are new** (discovery), (2) **what shape they have** (schema), (3) **what it already loaded** (state), so a retry or tomorrow's run doesn't load yesterday's files again.

items.def: Bringing data from outside the platform into it (here: files → Delta).
The source delivers data as files (CSV/JSON/Parquet…) in object storage or a Volume.
The storage path/Volume where source files arrive before ingestion.
Each run processes only what is new since the last run.
Re-running the pipeline on the same inputs gives the same table — no surprises, no duplicates.

sections.title: spark.read & CSV Parsing Options
sections.hook: A CSV file is a grammar — if you don't tell the parser the rules, it reads nonsense without complaining.

blocks.text: `spark.read` is the most basic PySpark ingestion API. It is a **batch read**: it reads what is in the path *right now*.

blocks.code: df = spark.read.format("json").load(path)

blocks.caption: What a batch read does

blocks.code:
orders = (
    spark.read
        .format("json")
        .load("/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/incoming/orders/")
)

# shorter, identical:
orders = spark.read.json("/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/incoming/orders/")
blocks.caption: Long form vs shorthand

blocks.title: Two spellings, one reader
blocks.text: `spark.read.format("csv").load(p)` ≡ `spark.read.csv(p)`; same for `json` and `parquet`. The long form is handy when the format is a variable.
**CSV** needs parsing options. The `header` option says: *the first line holds the column names*.

blocks.code:
df = (
    spark.read
        .format("csv")
        .option("header", "true")
        .load(path)
)
blocks.caption: CSV with header

blocks.code:
order_id,customer_id,amount
1001,17,25.90
1002,18,10.50
blocks.caption: orders.csv

blocks.text: **Delimiter**: CSV doesn't always mean comma. A pipe-separated file needs `.option("delimiter", "|")` (alias `sep`).

blocks.code:
# file:  1001|17|25.90
#        1002|18|10.50
df = (
    spark.read
        .format("csv")
        .option("delimiter", "|")
        .load(path)
)
blocks.caption: Pipe-delimited CSV

blocks.code:
.option("header", "true")
.option("delimiter", ",")
.option("quote", '"')
.option("escape", '"')
.option("multiLine", "true")
.option("nullValue", "NULL")
blocks.caption: Options you'll meet constantly

head: Option
Tells the parser…
Example problem it solves
rows: how a quote inside a quoted field is escaped
a quoted field may contain newlines
an address with a line break becomes 2 rows
what to do with malformed rows

blocks.text: **`mode`** (added for clarity — you need it to debug bad CSV): **PERMISSIVE** (default) keeps the row and sets unparsable fields to null; **DROPMALFORMED** silently drops bad rows; **FAILFAST** throws on the first bad row. In PERMISSIVE you can keep the raw bad line with `columnNameOfCorruptRecord` (e.g. `_corrupt_record`).

blocks.title: The file format is a grammar
blocks.text: Don't memorize every option. Learn to think: *what is the structure of this file, and have I told the parser?* Separator, quoting, escaping, line breaks, null spelling, header.

blocks.title: No header option → header becomes data
blocks.text: Reading a CSV with a header line but without `.option("header","true")` gives columns `_c0, _c1…` AND an extra data row containing the column names — which later fails every cast.

blocks.title: CSV without schema = all STRING
blocks.text: Plain CSV has no native types. With neither `.schema(...)` nor `inferSchema=true`, every CSV column is read as **STRING**.

blocks.label: Think first: you read `1001|17|25.90` with default CSV options. How many columns do you get?
blocks.text: **One** column `_c0` containing the whole line `1001|17|25.90` — the parser looked for commas, found none. No error is raised: wrong grammar silently gives wrong data.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a CSV reads wrong
questions: Did I set `header` — and does the file actually have a header line?
Is the separator really a comma, or `|`, `;`, tab?
Do fields contain the separator or newlines inside quotes (quote / escape / multiLine)?
How does the source spell NULL (`NULL`, empty, `NA`)?
Which `mode` decides what happens to malformed rows — and am I silently dropping or nulling data?

sections.title: Schema Inference vs Explicit Schema
sections.hook: Guessing types costs an extra pass over the data — and tomorrow's guess may differ from today's.

blocks.text: If you don't give a schema, Spark can **infer** one. For CSV you must ask for it with `inferSchema`.

blocks.code:
df = (
    spark.read
        .option("header", "true")
        .option("inferSchema", "true")
        .csv(path)
)

blocks.text: Why does inference **cost** something? To know whether `"123"` is INT, LONG or STRING, Spark must **look at the data** first.

blocks.caption: Inference = an extra pass

blocks.title: Explicit schema skips the inference pass
blocks.text: Databricks documentation says it explicitly: supplying a schema lets the reader **skip schema inference**, which speeds up the read.

blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql.types import (
    StructType, StructField,
    LongType, DoubleType, StringType, TimestampType,
)

schema = StructType([
    StructField("order_id",    LongType(),      True),
    StructField("customer_id", LongType(),      True),
    StructField("amount",      DoubleType(),    True),
    StructField("status",      StringType(),    True),
    StructField("order_ts",    TimestampType(), True),
])

df = spark.read.schema(schema).json(path)
blocks.caption: Explicit schema with StructType (the 3rd arg = nullable)

blocks.text: With `.schema(...)` you say: **"Don't guess. This is the contract."**

blocks.code:
schema = """
  order_id    BIGINT,
  customer_id BIGINT,
  amount      DOUBLE,
  status      STRING,
  order_ts    TIMESTAMP
"""

df = spark.read.schema(schema).json(path)
blocks.caption: Same contract as a DDL-formatted string

blocks.code:
schema = """
  order_id BIGINT, customer_id BIGINT,
  amount DOUBLE,   status STRING
"""

df = (
    spark.read
        .format("csv")
        .option("header", "true")
        .schema(schema)
        .load("/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/orders_csv/")
)
display(df)
blocks.caption: Lab: CSV ingestion with an explicit schema

blocks.text: Databricks accepts a schema either as a **StructType** or as a **DDL string**. The DDL string is often more readable and easy to review in Git.

items.title: Explicit schema
points: No accidental type surprises; easier validation

blocks.text:
File 1 (Mon)        File 2 (Tue)
 amount              amount
 100                 100.50
 200
   ↓ infer             ↓ infer
 amount: INT         amount: DOUBLE   ← type changed!
blocks.caption: The schema-inference bug: same column, different guess

blocks.title: Inference is a moving target
blocks.text: Monday's files make Spark infer `amount INT`; Tuesday's file has `100.50` → the inferred type changes (or parsing breaks). Downstream writes then hit schema mismatches.

blocks.title: Engineering question: why explicit schema in production?
blocks.text: It **avoids an inference pass**, gives a **stable data contract**, makes **failures predictable**, prevents **accidental type drift**, and lets schema changes be **reviewed** instead of silently inferred.

blocks.label: Think first: with an explicit schema `amount DOUBLE`, a row arrives with `amount = "abc"`. What happens in the default PERMISSIVE mode?
blocks.text: The row is kept and `amount` becomes **null** (optionally the raw record goes to a corrupt-record or rescued-data column). No type drift — the contract held; the bad *value* is what you now investigate.

blocks.title: Ask yourself before relying on schema inference
questions: Is this exploration or a production pipeline?
Would a different guess tomorrow (INT → DOUBLE) break a downstream write?
Who owns the contract with the upstream team — and is it written down?
Could a reviewer see a schema change in Git, or would it happen silently?

sections.title: JSON, Parquet & read_files()
sections.hook: Text formats need parsing, typed formats carry their schema — and SQL has its own file reader.

blocks.text: **JSON** (as read by Spark by default) is one object per line — *JSON Lines*:

blocks.code:
{"order_id": 1, "customer": "Maria", "amount": 20.5}
{"order_id": 2, "customer": "John",  "amount": 50.0}
blocks.caption: orders.json

blocks.code:
df = spark.read.json(path)                 # types inferred from values
df = spark.read.schema(schema).json(path)  # explicit contract

blocks.text: JSON can be **nested**. A nested object becomes a **struct** column:

blocks.code: {"order_id": 1, "customer": {"id": 100, "name": "Maria"}}

blocks.text:
root
  ├── order_id: long
  └── customer: struct
        ├── id: long
        └── name: string
blocks.caption: Inferred schema (printSchema) — access with customer.name

blocks.title: One record spread over many lines?
blocks.text: Pretty-printed JSON (one object across several lines, or a big array) needs `.option("multiLine", "true")`; the default reader expects one JSON object per line.
**Parquet** is typed: each file stores its **schema metadata**. `spark.read.parquet(path)` needs no CSV-style parsing options or type guessing.

head: Format
Nature
Where types come from
rows: weak / none — you or inference decide

blocks.text: That's why lakehouses typically **ingest raw CSV/JSON** and then write **Delta (Parquet-backed) tables**: from then on the types live with the data.
**`read_files()`** is Databricks' SQL table-valued function for reading files. It reads CSV, JSON, XML, text, binary, Parquet, Avro and ORC, and can infer format and schema.

blocks.caption: read_files: inferred vs explicit schema (named args use =>)

blocks.text: Where you'll use it: **Databricks SQL**, **Lakeflow pipelines**, and **ad-hoc file exploration**.

blocks.code:
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_orders
AS
SELECT *
FROM STREAM read_files(
  '/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/orders/',
  format => 'json'
);
blocks.caption: Preview of Phase 6: read_files inside a streaming table

blocks.title: STREAM read_files = Auto Loader underneath
blocks.text: When `read_files` is used with `STREAM` in a streaming table, Databricks runs **Auto Loader** for incremental file ingestion. Everything you learn about Auto Loader (checkpoints, schema inference, rescued data) applies.

blocks.label: Think first: why does Parquet not need a `header` or `inferSchema` option?
blocks.text: Because the **schema is stored in the file** itself (column names + types in the footer). There's nothing to guess and no header line to interpret.

sections.title: Metadata Columns: Which File Did This Row Come From?
sections.hook: When a bad row shows up in Silver, the first question is 'which file?' — make Bronze able to answer.

blocks.text: When you ingest files you often want to know: **from which file did this row come? when was the file created? which source sent it?**

business data          +   ingestion metadata
 order_id, amount           _source_file, _ingested_at
blocks.caption: A Bronze row = what the source said + how it got here

blocks.text: Spark file sources expose a hidden **`_metadata`** column. You must **select it explicitly** — `SELECT *` doesn't include it.

head: Field
Meaning
rows: Full path of the source file
Last modification timestamp of the file

blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

bronze_df = (
    spark.read.schema(schema).json(path)
        .select(
            "*",
            F.col("_metadata.file_path").alias("_source_file"),
            F.current_timestamp().alias("_ingested_at"),
        )
)
blocks.caption: Adding audit columns (works the same on an Auto Loader stream)

blocks.code:
SELECT *, _metadata.file_path AS _source_file
FROM read_files('/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/orders/', format => 'json');
blocks.caption: Same idea in SQL

blocks.title: Legacy spelling
blocks.text: Older code uses `input_file_name()`. Prefer `_metadata.file_path`: it's the current, documented way and also gives size and modification time.

Silver bad row
      ↓  (keys / lineage)
 Bronze source row  ── _source_file = .../orders_0912.json
      ↓
 original file in the landing zone
blocks.caption: Audit trail that metadata columns make possible

blocks.title: Source-file metadata = audit evidence
blocks.text: Good Bronze systems add `_source_file` and `_ingestion_ts`/`_ingested_at`. When someone asks *"where did this bad record come from?"*, you answer with a query, not a guess. That's operational observability.

blocks.title: _metadata isn't in SELECT *
blocks.text: The `_metadata` column is hidden: `select("*")` or `SELECT *` won't return it, so audit columns silently go missing.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a Silver row looks wrong
questions: Which Bronze row produced it (same business key, same batch)?
What is that Bronze row's `_source_file`?
When was it ingested (`_ingested_at`) — before or after the incident?
Is the original file still in the landing zone, and unchanged?

sections.title: The Re-read Problem → COPY INTO Idempotency
sections.hook: spark.read has no memory: run it twice and you load everything twice. COPY INTO remembers files.

blocks.text: Day 1: folder `orders/` has `file1.json`, `file2.json`. You run `spark.read.json(path)` and append to Bronze. Day 2 a `file3.json` lands. You run the same code. **What does it read?**

Day 1 run           Day 2 run
 orders/             orders/
 ├── file1  ✔        ├── file1  ✔  (again!)
 └── file2  ✔        ├── file2  ✔  (again!)
                     └── file3  ✔
blocks.caption: spark.read reads the whole current folder every time

blocks.text: **All three files** — not just `file3`. Appended to Bronze, file1 and file2 are now **duplicated**. That's the core problem of incremental ingestion.

blocks.code:
(
    df.write
      .mode("append")
      .saveAsTable("ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw")
)
# run twice over the same files  →  duplicate rows
blocks.caption: Lab: plain batch load — run it twice on purpose

blocks.title: No file-history memory
blocks.text: Plain `spark.read` keeps **no record** of which files it has seen. Re-reading the same source file and appending = duplicates. The duplication is the intended lesson of the lab.
**Naive fix**: restrict the path by date, e.g. `path = "/orders/2026-09-28/*.json"`. It works only if the **upstream storage layout is perfectly reliable**.

items: **Late files** — yesterday's file lands after today's run started
**Re-uploads** — same day folder gets a corrected file
**Timezone bugs** — '2026-09-28' in UTC vs local time
**Missing expected folders** — the job fails or silently loads nothing

blocks.title: Date-folder filtering is fragile incremental logic
blocks.text: Filtering by filename/date assumes a perfect upstream layout. Late files, backfills, re-uploads, timezone bugs, renames and missing folders all cause skipped or duplicated data.
**`COPY INTO`** is the first Databricks ingestion primitive with memory. It loads files into a **Delta table** and is **retryable and idempotent**: files already loaded are **skipped** on later runs.

Run 1: file1, file2 present  → load file1, load file2
 Run 2: nothing new           → skip file1, skip file2
 file3.json lands
 Run 3:                       → skip file1, skip file2, load file3
blocks.caption: Idempotent = safe to re-run

blocks.text: Compare that with naive *read the entire folder every run*: re-running COPY INTO after a failure or by accident doesn't duplicate anything.

blocks.title: A changed file is still 'already loaded'
blocks.text: Databricks: if a file was already loaded, COPY INTO **skips it on later runs even if the file's contents have changed**. Same tracked file identity ≠ 'reload because content changed'.

**`force`** (added for clarity): `COPY_OPTIONS ('force' = 'true')` disables the idempotency check and loads the files again *regardless* of history — useful for a deliberate reload, dangerous by accident (duplicates).
The **target must be a Delta table**. You can create it with a schema first:

blocks.code:
COPY INTO ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw
FROM '/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/orders_csv/'
FILEFORMAT = CSV
FORMAT_OPTIONS (
  'header'    = 'true',
  'delimiter' = ','
);
blocks.caption: CSV COPY INTO: parser options go in FORMAT_OPTIONS

blocks.code:
COPY INTO ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw
FROM '/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/orders_csv/'
FILEFORMAT = CSV
FORMAT_OPTIONS ('header' = 'true', 'inferSchema' = 'true');
-- run it twice: the 2nd run skips the already-loaded files
blocks.caption: Lab: clear/rebuild the table, then run COPY INTO twice

blocks.label: Think first: you re-run the exact same COPY INTO 5 minutes later and no new files arrived. How many rows are added?
blocks.text: **Zero.** Every file is already in COPY INTO's load history, so all are skipped. The statement still succeeds — that's what idempotent means.

blocks.title: Ask yourself before re-running a load
questions: Does this tool remember which files it loaded (COPY INTO / Auto Loader) or not (spark.read)?
If a file was corrected upstream, did it arrive as a NEW file or overwrite the old one?
Am I about to use `force` — and what will dedupe the duplicates it creates?
Is my target a Delta table?

sections.title: COPY INTO Options: PATTERN, FILES, VALIDATE, Transforms & Schema
sections.hook: COPY INTO isn't a byte copy: it filters, validates, casts and can evolve the target schema.

blocks.text: **PATTERN** filters which source files are loaded. Folder `incoming/` holds `orders_001.csv`, `orders_002.csv`, `customers_001.csv` — you want only orders:

blocks.code:
COPY INTO ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw
FROM '/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/incoming/'
FILEFORMAT = CSV
PATTERN = 'orders_*.csv'
FORMAT_OPTIONS ('header' = 'true');

blocks.title: PATTERN is a glob, not a regex
blocks.text: COPY INTO's PATTERN is a **glob pattern** (`*`, `?`, `[a-z]`, `{a,b}`). The tutoring notes wrote a regex-style `'orders_.*[.]csv'` — as a glob that means 'orders_.' + anything + '.csv' and would NOT match `orders_001.csv`.
**FILES** loads an explicit list of file names (relative to the FROM path) — up to **1000 files per statement**. FILES and PATTERN can't be combined in one statement.

blocks.code:
COPY INTO ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw
FROM '/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/orders/'
FILEFORMAT = JSON
FILES = ('file1.json', 'file2.json');

blocks.text: **VALIDATE** checks the files **without writing data**: do they parse, is the schema compatible (or evolvable), do nullability and CHECK constraints hold?

blocks.code:
COPY INTO ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw
FROM '/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/orders_csv/'
FILEFORMAT = CSV
FORMAT_OPTIONS ('header' = 'true')
VALIDATE ALL;      -- or: VALIDATE 15 ROWS
blocks.caption: Lab: validate first, inspect the result, then load

blocks.title: A pre-production / debugging tool
blocks.text: Run `VALIDATE ALL` against a new feed or a suspicious batch before the real load. Nothing is committed, so it's safe on production targets.
COPY INTO can **transform** while loading — the FROM can be a SELECT over the files: projection, casts, functions, even metadata.

blocks.code:
COPY INTO ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw
FROM (
  SELECT
    order_id::BIGINT,
    customer_id::BIGINT,
    amount::DOUBLE,
    upper(status)        AS status,
    _metadata.file_path  AS _source_file
  FROM '/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/orders/'
)
FILEFORMAT = JSON;

blocks.title: Not a byte copy
blocks.text: COPY INTO parses files and can project, cast and compute columns. The target still gets typed Delta rows.

blocks.code:
COPY INTO ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw
FROM '/path/'
FILEFORMAT = CSV
FORMAT_OPTIONS ('inferSchema' = 'true', 'mergeSchema' = 'true')
COPY_OPTIONS ('mergeSchema' = 'true');
blocks.caption: Inference + schema evolution in COPY INTO

head: Where
mergeSchema means…
rows: Merge the schemas of the **source files** (file A has col x, file B has col y → read both)
**Evolve the target Delta table's** schema to accept new columns

blocks.title: Two different mergeSchema options
blocks.text: `FORMAT_OPTIONS mergeSchema` reconciles schemas across source files; `COPY_OPTIONS mergeSchema` evolves the target Delta schema. Setting only one may not give you new columns in the table.

Nice trick (added for clarity): you can create a **schemaless placeholder** Delta table with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw;` and let COPY INTO with `mergeSchema` set the schema on first load.

blocks.label: Think first: you use FILES with 2,500 file names. What happens?
blocks.text: One statement accepts at most **1000** file names, so you split into **3 statements** (1000 + 1000 + 500) — or use a PATTERN / let idempotency pick new files instead.

sections.title: Auto Loader: cloudFiles, readStream & the Bronze Skeleton
sections.hook: When the folder holds millions of files and keeps growing, you need discovery with memory — that's Auto Loader.

blocks.text: Databricks' guidance on scale: **thousands of files over time → COPY INTO can be fine; millions+ → prefer Auto Loader**. Auto Loader discovers files more efficiently, processes them in incremental batches and has richer schema inference/evolution.
The problem: `orders/` holds **5,000,000** files and **+100** arrive every 10 seconds. A naive loader lists all 5,000,000 names each time to find the 100 new ones.

every trigger:
   list 5,000,000 names  ──►  compare with what I loaded  ──►  100 new
   (cost grows with the folder, not with the new data)
blocks.caption: Naive discovery doesn't scale

blocks.text: **Auto Loader** keeps **incremental state** about what it has already discovered and processed, so work scales with new arrivals.

blocks.code:
orders = (
    spark.readStream
        .format("cloudFiles")
        .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
        .load("/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/orders/")
)
blocks.caption: Auto Loader read

blocks.title: `cloudFiles` = Auto Loader
blocks.text: The magic identifier `format("cloudFiles")` means *use Auto Loader*. The actual file format goes in `cloudFiles.format`.

**Why `readStream`?** Auto Loader is built on **Spark Structured Streaming**. That doesn't mean the source is Kafka or a live event feed — the source is **files**. The *processing model* is streaming: incremental arrivals → micro-batches of new files.

blocks.caption: Streaming as a processing model, not a source type

blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

source_path     = "/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/orders/"
schema_path     = "/Volumes/ecommerce/system/orders_schema/"
checkpoint_path = "/Volumes/ecommerce/system/orders_checkpoint/"

orders = (
    spark.readStream
        .format("cloudFiles")
        .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
        .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", schema_path)
        .load(source_path)
        .withColumn("_ingested_at", F.current_timestamp())
)

query = (
    orders.writeStream
        .format("delta")
        .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint_path)
        .toTable("ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw")
)
blocks.caption: Production-style Bronze ingestion skeleton — memorize this shape

head: Piece
Role
rows: Format of the files (json, csv, parquet…)
Where inferred schema + its history are stored

blocks.text: **Lab:** start the stream, drop a new file into `orders_json/`, and observe that **only the new arrival** is processed.

items.title: Misconception
points: Auto Loader turns files into Kafka

items.title: Reality
points: Its edge is **incremental discovery + state tracking + schema handling + streaming integration**, not reading each file faster
The **source stays files**; only the processing model is streaming/incremental

blocks.title: Auto Loader is not 'faster spark.read'
blocks.text: Auto Loader doesn't read an individual file faster. Its value is incremental file discovery, remembered state, schema handling and streaming integration.

blocks.label: Think first: where does the word `json` go in an Auto Loader read — `.format("json")`?
blocks.text: No. `.format("cloudFiles")` selects Auto Loader; the file format goes in **`.option("cloudFiles.format", "json")`**. Writing `.format("json")` with readStream gives a plain file stream without Auto Loader's features.

sections.title: schemaLocation vs checkpointLocation & What Happens Inside
sections.hook: Two folders, two memories: one remembers the SHAPE of the data, the other remembers HOW FAR you got.

blocks.text: An Auto Loader pipeline has **two state locations**. Beginners mix them up constantly.

cloudFiles.schemaLocation          checkpointLocation
 ─────────────────────────          ──────────────────────────
 "What SHAPE does the data have?"   "How FAR has this stream got?"
  • schema I inferred                • files already processed
  • how it evolved                   • offsets / batch ids
  • schema versions  (_schemas/)     • stream metadata & state
 set on the READ (cloudFiles.*)     set on the WRITE (writeStream)
blocks.caption: Different questions, different owners

blocks.text: **schemaLocation**: Auto Loader must remember *which schema it discovered, how it evolved, which versions existed*. Databricks stores the inferred schema in a **`_schemas`** folder under `cloudFiles.schemaLocation`.
**checkpointLocation**: the streaming query's **progress and state** — conceptually *files processed: A, B, C* plus stream metadata — so a restart continues correctly.

blocks.title: Same directory is allowed, same role is not
blocks.text: Databricks examples sometimes point both options at the same directory (the schema goes into its `_schemas` subfolder). That works — but the two *roles* stay different: schema history vs stream progress.

blocks.title: schemaLocation ≠ progress
blocks.text: `cloudFiles.schemaLocation` stores **schema history/state**, not stream progress. Progress lives in the **checkpoint**. Exam questions swap them on purpose.

files:   A   B   C
 stream:  A ✔ B ✔ ──✖ cluster dies
 checkpoint: "A, B done"
 restart  ──►  reads checkpoint  ──►  processes C only
blocks.caption: Restart: continue, don't start from zero

blocks.title: What exactly does the checkpoint protect?
blocks.text: It stores the streaming query's **progress and state**, so after a restart the query continues from the correct point instead of rediscovering the input as if it were new.

blocks.title: Checkpoint on ephemeral disk
blocks.text: `checkpointLocation="/tmp/checkpoint"` lives on a worker's local disk. When the cluster terminates, the checkpoint vanishes → the stream loses all progress.

**Do I still need schemaLocation with an explicit schema?** If you fully provide `.schema(...)` and don't use Auto Loader-managed inference/evolution, schemaLocation isn't required in the same way. Whenever Auto Loader **infers or evolves** the schema, `cloudFiles.schemaLocation` is critical. The **checkpoint is always required** for the write.

blocks.title: The heart of Auto Loader
blocks.text: Commit the Delta transaction, *then* advance the checkpoint. That ordering is why a crash in between doesn't lose or double-count files when the sink is Delta.

blocks.label: Think first: a stream processed A and B, then the cluster died. The checkpoint is intact. File C arrived meanwhile. What happens on restart?
blocks.text: Auto Loader reads the checkpoint (A, B done), discovers C as new and processes **only C**. It does not start from zero.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when setting up a new Auto Loader stream
questions: Is my checkpoint on persistent storage (Volume / cloud path), not /tmp?
Is this checkpoint path used by this one query only?
Am I inferring the schema — then where is schemaLocation?
Would I be able to explain which of the two folders holds what?

sections.title: Checkpoint Incidents: Deleted, Shared, Re-pointed
sections.hook: A checkpoint is operational state, not a cache — delete it, share it or re-point it and the stream forgets or confuses its past.

blocks.text: **Classic incident:** A, B, C are processed. Someone deletes the checkpoint ("cleanup"). The next start has **no ingestion history**.

before:  checkpoint = {A, B, C}     Bronze = A B C
 rm -r checkpoint
 restart: checkpoint = {}            sees A B C (+D) as NEW
          Bronze = A B C  A B C D   ← duplicates
blocks.caption: Deleted checkpoint → files may be seen as new

blocks.text: Depending on the pipeline and sink you may **duplicate ingestion** or need **recovery/reconciliation**.

blocks.title: Checkpoint = operational state
blocks.text: Deleting, resetting or moving a checkpoint wipes the stream's memory of what it processed. Re-ingestion and duplicates follow.

**Recovery options** (decide deliberately): restore the checkpoint if you have a copy; or restart fresh and **reconcile** — e.g. delete Bronze rows of re-ingested files by `_source_file`, or dedupe/MERGE downstream; or start a new checkpoint with `cloudFiles.includeExistingFiles = false` so only files arriving *after* the start are ingested (risk: files that landed during the gap are skipped).

Pipeline A ──┐
              ├──► checkpoint=/shared/checkpoint   ✖ corrupt state
 Pipeline B ──┘
blocks.caption: Two queries, one checkpoint

blocks.title: Shared checkpoint path
blocks.text: Two unrelated streaming queries writing to the same checkpoint location can corrupt each other's progress and state: one may skip files, the other reprocess, or the stream fails.

**Re-pointing the source**: the checkpoint belonged to a query reading `/orders/sourceA`. You change the code to read `/orders/sourceB` but keep the same checkpoint. **Dangerous** — the checkpoint describes the logical query and its source topology, not a generic cache.

blocks.title: Changed source, same checkpoint
blocks.text: Keeping a checkpoint after changing the source path (or other topology) mixes the old query's progress with a new input: files can be skipped, re-read or the stream can fail.

blocks.title: Ask yourself whenever a stream's history looks wrong
questions: Is the checkpoint location exactly the same as in the last good run?
Was the checkpoint deleted, moved or overwritten (deploy, cleanup script, path typo)?
Does any other query write to the same checkpoint path?
Did the source path or query shape change while the checkpoint stayed the same?
Do Bronze rows show old `_source_file`s with new `_ingested_at` values?

sections.title: File Discovery & Auto Loader Schema Inference
sections.hook: How Auto Loader finds new files, and why its default schema is all STRING — on purpose.

blocks.text: Auto Loader must learn **which new files appeared**. Two conceptual mechanisms:

items.title: Directory listing
points: Can get expensive with huge file counts

items.title: File notification / managed file events
points: Auto Loader learns about it from events
Classic: `cloudFiles.useNotifications`; current: managed file events on UC external locations

blocks.text:
LISTING:       list path → diff vs state → new files
 NOTIFICATION:  new file → cloud event → Auto Loader knows

blocks.title: The takeaway that won't change
blocks.text: Exact cloud-specific implementations evolve; the concept stays: Auto Loader can **discover new files incrementally without a full directory scan each time**.
Auto Loader supports schema inference/evolution for **JSON, CSV, XML, Avro and Parquet** — with different semantics for text vs typed formats.
For **JSON, CSV and XML** Auto Loader infers every field as **STRING** by default — to reduce schema-evolution failures from type mismatches. Typed formats (Parquet, Avro) keep their encoded types.

blocks.code: .option("cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes", "true")
blocks.caption: Ask for real types instead

blocks.title: Auto Loader defaults text formats to STRING
blocks.text: Unlike `spark.read` with inferSchema, Auto Loader infers JSON/CSV/XML columns as STRING unless `cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes=true`.

today:     amount = 19.50        tomorrow:  amount = "unknown"
 Bronze amount DOUBLE  → parse fails / value rescued
 Bronze amount STRING  → keeps "19.50" and "unknown"  ✔
                         → Silver validates & casts
blocks.caption: Why Bronze often prefers strings
Medallion philosophy

blocks.text: **Initial inference samples**, it doesn't scan your whole history: by default up to **50 GB or 1000 files, whichever limit is reached first** (tunable via `cloudFiles.schemaInference.sampleSize.numBytes` / `.numFiles`).
**Schema hints** let you steer inference for specific columns without declaring every column:

blocks.code: .option("cloudFiles.schemaHints", "order_id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE")

blocks.text: For **typed formats like Parquet**, a hint tells the reader *which type to read the column as* — it is **not** just a cast applied after reading. `schema hint ≠ withColumn(cast(...))`.

blocks.title: Inferred once, remembered after
blocks.text: Inference runs when the stream first builds its schema and the result is persisted in schemaLocation. Flipping `inferColumnTypes` later on an existing stream doesn't magically re-infer the stored schema.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when Auto Loader columns come out as STRING
questions: Is the source JSON/CSV/XML, where STRING is the default?
Did I set `cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes` before the schema was first persisted?
Do I actually want raw strings in Bronze and typed casts in Silver?
Which few columns need types now — would schema hints be enough?

blocks.label: Think first: a vendor sends 3,000 JSON files of 10 MB each. Which sampling limit stops initial inference first?
blocks.text: **1000 files** (10 GB) is reached long before 50 GB. Inference sees only the first 1000 files — a column that appears only in later files isn't in the initial schema (schema evolution handles it later).

sections.title: Schema Evolution, Rescued Data & Quarantine
sections.hook: When the source changes shape, you want control — not a silent mutation and not lost data.

blocks.text: Yesterday: `order_id, amount`. Today the source adds **`discount_code`**. Auto Loader can detect and **evolve** the schema — depending on the configured mode.

new unexpected column discovered
          ↓
 Auto Loader records the schema change (schemaLocation)
          ↓
 stream FAILS / stops (default mode)
          ↓
 restart → new schema used, column included
blocks.caption: Why schema evolution can stop a stream

blocks.title: Stopping is a feature
blocks.text: In many production contexts this is desirable: **don't silently mutate pipeline semantics without control.** Run the stream under a Job with retries so the restart picks up the new schema.

head: cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode
On a new column…
rows: Stream fails; new column added to the schema; restart continues with it
Schema never evolves; stream keeps running; new columns go to the rescued data column
Stream fails and stays failed until you update the schema or remove the file
none (default when you provide a schema)
Schema doesn't evolve, new columns ignored (not rescued unless rescuedDataColumn is set)
blocks.caption: Modes added for clarity — the source says 'depending on configured mode'

blocks.code: .option("cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode", "addNewColumns")   # or rescue / failOnNewColumns / none

blocks.title: A failing stream after a new column isn't (necessarily) a bug
blocks.text: With the default addNewColumns mode, the first batch that contains a new column stops the stream after recording the new schema. Restarting picks it up.
**Rescued data** is one of Databricks' best ingestion ideas. Expected schema `id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE`; incoming:

blocks.code: {"id": 10, "amount": "UNKNOWN", "new_field": "abc"}

blocks.caption: Conceptual rescued row: nothing is lost

blocks.text: Instead of silently throwing away mismatched or unexpected fields, Auto Loader / `read_files` put them in a **rescued data column** (`_rescued_data`) — values that don't match the expected type, and fields not in the schema.

items.title: With rescue
points: Silver can inspect, alert, quarantine, fix

blocks.text:
Robust Bronze row
 ├── business/source fields : order_id, customer_id, amount, status
 ├── _ingested_at           : ingestion timestamp
 ├── _source_file           : source filename
 └── _rescued_data          : whatever didn't fit
blocks.caption: Bronze architecture pattern = excellent auditability

blocks.text:
Bronze
   ↓ validation
   ├── _rescued_data IS NULL     → Silver
   └── _rescued_data IS NOT NULL → quarantine.orders_bad
blocks.caption: Quarantine pattern

blocks.code:
bronze = spark.read.table("ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw")

(bronze.where("_rescued_data IS NOT NULL")
       .write.mode("append")
       .saveAsTable("ecommerce.quarantine.orders_bad"))

clean = bronze.where("_rescued_data IS NULL")   # continues to Silver

blocks.text: **Explicit schema with Auto Loader** — very common when the upstream contract is known. Note the deliberate STRING for `amount` and `order_ts`:

blocks.code:
schema = """
  order_id    BIGINT,
  customer_id BIGINT,
  amount      STRING,
  status      STRING,
  order_ts    STRING
"""

orders = (
    spark.readStream
        .format("cloudFiles")
        .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
        .schema(schema)
        .option("rescuedDataColumn", "_rescued_data")   # keep what doesn't fit
        .load(source)
)

blocks.title: Explicit schema hides new columns
blocks.text: With a strict explicit schema the evolution mode defaults to `none`: a new upstream column does NOT appear as a regular column and isn't rescued unless you set `rescuedDataColumn`.

items: **Lab — schema evolution:** start with `{"id":1,"amount":"20.0"}`, then add `{"id":2,"amount":"25.0","discount":"SAVE10"}`. Watch schemaLocation get a new schema version and the stream stop/restart.

**Lab — bad data:** add `{"id":3,"amount":{"unexpected":true}}`. If `amount` is typed (hint/inferColumnTypes), the object can't fit → `amount` null + value in `_rescued_data`. If `amount` is STRING it may simply be kept as raw JSON text. Either way: **don't just make it pass — know where unexpected data goes.**

blocks.title: Ask yourself when an Auto Loader stream stops on a schema change
questions: Is this the documented addNewColumns stop-and-restart, not a real failure?
Which file introduced the new column, and is the change intentional?
Does schemaLocation now hold a new schema version?
Should this feed evolve, rescue, or fail loudly?
Will a job retry restart the stream automatically?

blocks.label: Think first: why is quarantining by `_rescued_data IS NOT NULL` better than dropping those rows in Bronze?
blocks.text: Because Bronze keeps the evidence. Quarantine isolates suspicious rows from Silver while preserving them for alerting, investigation and reprocessing once the rule or the source is fixed.

sections.title: Exactly-once, Bronze → MERGE & Production Architecture
sections.hook: Each file loaded once is not the same as each order stored once — know which layer guarantees what.

blocks.text: Auto Loader is designed for **exactly-once file ingestion** into Delta — when combined correctly with checkpointing and a supported (transactional) sink.
That does **not** mean duplicates can never appear in your business table. Duplicates can come from the **source data itself**:

file A: order_id=100        file B: order_id=100
   processed once ✔            processed once ✔
              ↓                       ↓
     Bronze: two rows with order_id = 100   (correctly!)

 file-level exactly-once  ≠  business-key deduplication

blocks.title: Auto Loader tracks FILES, not business entities
blocks.text: `fileA processed once` + `fileB processed once` does not imply `order_id 100 appears once`. Business-key dedup/upsert is Silver's job.

blocks.title: Exactly-once ≠ no duplicate keys
blocks.text: Exactly-once file ingestion guarantees each *file* is ingested once. Two distinct files (an upstream retry, a resend, an update) can legitimately contain the same order_id.

blocks.caption: Common architecture

blocks.text: This cleanly separates **ingestion correctness** (every file exactly once) from **business-state correctness** (every order once, latest version).

blocks.code:
MERGE INTO ecommerce.silver.orders AS t
USING (
  SELECT *
  FROM ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw
  QUALIFY row_number() OVER (
    PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY _ingested_at DESC) = 1
) AS s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;
blocks.caption: Sketch: dedupe Bronze by business key, then MERGE into Silver (column lists simplified)

items.title: Better
points: **Silver**: validate, dedup, cast, join, apply CDC
Recovery is easy: fix Silver code, rebuild from Bronze

blocks.title: Transforming (and dropping) during ingestion
blocks.text: Bronze that applies business rules, joins and drops malformed rows loses the raw evidence; when a rule is wrong you can't rebuild.

blocks.title: Why not write Auto Loader directly into Silver?
blocks.text: Bronze gives **source fidelity, replay, audit, schema-drift handling, rescued data and debugging**. Silver then enforces **business keys, types, deduplication, CDC and quality**. The separation minimizes coupling between ingestion and business transformation.

Cloud / Volume landing zone
   ↓  immutable files
 Auto Loader
   ↓
 Bronze  : raw + metadata + rescued data
   ↓  validation
 Silver  : typed + dedup + CDC
   ↓
 Gold
blocks.caption: The production ingestion architecture to internalize

blocks.text: **Production assignment** — build `/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/orders/` → Auto Loader → `ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw` with `order_id, customer_id, amount, status, _ingested_at, _rescued_data`, then deliberately test:

items: Delete the checkpoint — in a sandbox only
Add a duplicate business key in a different file
Verify Auto Loader processes each file once
Prove the business duplicate still exists

blocks.label: Think first: in step 14 the duplicate order_id is still in Bronze although every file was processed exactly once. Is Auto Loader broken?
blocks.text: No. Two **different files** each contained order_id 100, and each file was correctly ingested once. File identity ≠ business identity — step 15 (dedupe downstream) is where that's fixed.

sections.title: Choosing the Tool: spark.read vs COPY INTO vs Auto Loader
sections.hook: Same goal, three tools — pick by file count, arrival pattern, schema churn and who writes the code.

blocks.text: Sometimes you don't want a permanently running stream. You want: **process all new files now, then stop.** That's the **AvailableNow** trigger.

blocks.caption: AvailableNow

blocks.code:
query = (
    orders.writeStream
        .format("delta")
        .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint_path)
        .trigger(availableNow=True)
        .toTable("ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw")
)
query.awaitTermination()   # optional: block until done
blocks.caption: Scheduled, batch-like incremental ingestion with Auto Loader

blocks.title: Streaming engine, batch-like job
blocks.text: AvailableNow shows that the streaming engine can implement **batch-like incremental jobs**: schedule it hourly in a Job, it catches up and stops — with checkpoint guarantees and no always-on cluster.

items.title: Use COPY INTO when
points: moderate number of files (thousands over time)

head: Property
spark.read
COPY INTO
Auto Loader
blocks.caption: The comparison table

blocks.title: Millions of files arriving continuously
blocks.text: Exam: 'millions of files arriving continuously in cloud object storage — which mechanism?' Answer: **Auto Loader** — not repeated spark.read, and typically not COPY INTO at that scale.

blocks.label: Think first: a team with SQL-only analysts gets ~20 CSV files a day from a partner and occasionally must reload one specific file. Which tool?
blocks.text: **COPY INTO**: moderate volume, SQL-centric, idempotent re-runs, and `FILES = (...)` (+ `force` when deliberate) handles the selective reload.

sections.title: Debugging I: Missing Rows & Overwritten Files
sections.hook: 'New files exist but no rows appear' has eight possible breakpoints — check them in order.

blocks.text: Symptom: the landing zone has new files, Bronze has **no new rows**. Don't guess — walk the chain from the source to the sink:

blocks.caption: Systematic order: source → sink

head: Breakpoint
Typical evidence
rows: Upstream says 'sent', listing of the path shows nothing
cloudFiles.format json, files are `.csv` / `.json.gz` / filtered out
Same file names as before (overwrite) → checkpoint says done
Stream stopped on schema change; rows rejected

blocks.title: Ask yourself when new files exist but no rows appear
questions: Do the new files actually exist where I think (list the path)?
Does the stream's `.load()` path exactly match where they land?
Are the extension and format what the reader expects?
Did Auto Loader discover them (query progress: numFilesOutstanding / input rows)?
Does the checkpoint consider them already processed (same names, overwritten)?
Did parsing fail (nulls, `_rescued_data`, corrupt records)?
Is the stream stopped on a schema change?
Did the write to the sink fail (permissions, table changed)?

blocks.text: **File accidentally overwritten**: COPY INTO may still treat a previously loaded file as processed **even if its contents changed** — the correction never arrives. Auto Loader behaves similarly by default (it doesn't reprocess modified files unless `cloudFiles.allowOverwrites` is enabled, which risks duplicates).

blocks.title: Overwriting source files in place
blocks.text: Incremental loaders reason about **file identity**. An overwritten file may be skipped as 'already loaded' (lost correction) or, with overwrites allowed, reprocessed (duplicates).

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a corrected source file doesn't show up
questions: Was the correction delivered as a new file or as an overwrite of a loaded one?
Does the loader consider that file identity already processed?
Is the file's modification time later than its rows' `_ingested_at`?
If I force a reload, what removes the old rows first?

blocks.title: Immutable landing zones are easier to reason about
blocks.text: Incremental systems reason much more reliably about **new file identities** than about mutable files.

sections.title: Debugging II: Schema Shifts, Missing Columns, Duplicate IDs & Bad CSV
sections.hook: Four incidents you will meet in your first month — each with its own ordered questions.

blocks.text: **Schema suddenly changes.** Yesterday `amount STRING`; today the source sends `amount` as a **STRUCT**.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when the source schema suddenly changes
questions: Was the source contract intentionally changed?
Did only one corrupt file do this?
Should the field be rescued?
Should the schema evolve?
Should the stream fail?

blocks.title: Don't blindly allow everything
blocks.text: Turning on every evolution option lets an accidental upstream change (e.g. amount becoming a struct) flow silently into Silver and Gold.
**New column missing.** Upstream adds `discount`, but Bronze doesn't show it. Check: **schema evolution mode**, **schemaLocation state**, a **provided explicit schema**, **rescued data**.

blocks.title: Explicit schema swallows new columns
blocks.text: If you supplied a strict explicit schema, a new field won't appear as a regular column automatically (mode `none`). Look in `_rescued_data` — if you enabled it.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a new upstream column is missing
questions: Which schemaEvolutionMode is in effect?
What does the latest schema in schemaLocation contain?
Am I providing a strict explicit schema without the new field?
Is the value sitting in `_rescued_data` — is rescue even enabled?

blocks.text: **Duplicated business IDs.** Rows show `order_id=100` twice. **Do not immediately blame Auto Loader.**

head: Question
If yes →
rows: Ingestion problem (checkpoint reset, force, plain re-read)
Two different files both contain the ID?
Silver MERGE/dedup missing or wrong key?

blocks.title: File idempotency vs business-key idempotency
blocks.text: This is exactly why we separate **file idempotency** (Auto Loader / COPY INTO) from **business-key idempotency** (dedup / MERGE in Silver).

blocks.title: Ask yourself when you see duplicated business IDs
questions: Was the same source file loaded twice?
Do two different files both contain the ID?
Was it an upstream retry?
Is the Silver MERGE/dedup missing or keyed wrongly?
Was a checkpoint reset?

blocks.text: **Malformed CSV.** Expected `id,amount` / `1,10.5`. Bad line: `2,"10.5` — an **unclosed quote**.

Possible results: **parse error**, **corrupt/rescued data**, or **unexpected columns** (the quote swallows the separator and the next line). Investigate the parser options: `quote`, `escape`, `multiLine`, `delimiter`, `header`.

blocks.code:
df = (
    spark.read
        .format("csv")
        .option("header", "true")
        .option("quote", '"')
        .option("escape", '"')
        .option("multiLine", "true")
        .option("mode", "PERMISSIVE")
        .option("columnNameOfCorruptRecord", "_corrupt_record")
        .schema("id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE, _corrupt_record STRING")
        .load(path)
)
blocks.caption: Make bad lines visible instead of guessing

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a CSV has malformed rows
questions: What does the raw line look like?
Is there an unclosed or unescaped quote (quote / escape)?
Do quoted fields contain newlines (multiLine)?
Are delimiter and header right?
Is my mode hiding bad rows (DROPMALFORMED) or surfacing them?

blocks.title: multiLine + broken quote = swallowed rows
blocks.text: With `multiLine=true`, an unclosed quote can make the parser treat the following lines as part of one field — several good rows can vanish into one bad record.

debug.title: Inferred column types drift between runs
debug.symptom: Yesterday's load worked; today the write fails with a schema mismatch, or `amount` arrives as DOUBLE/STRING instead of INT. Nobody changed the code.
askYourself: Is this read using `inferSchema` (or JSON's default inference) instead of an explicit schema?
What type did yesterday's run infer, and what does today's run infer for the same column?
Which new file introduced the different values (e.g. `100.50`, `unknown`)?
Is the new value legitimate (contract change) or a bad record?
Should Bronze keep this column as STRING and cast in Silver instead?

steps.do: Print both schemas and diff them.
steps.why: Confirms it's an inference change, not a code change.

steps.do: Find the file with the new value pattern using the source-file path.
Ask the upstream owner whether the type change is intended.
Replace inference with an explicit schema (DDL string) in Git.
steps.code:
schema = "order_id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE, status STRING"
df = spark.read.schema(schema).json(path)

rootCauses: Schema inferred from different samples each run
debug.fix: Pin the contract: explicit schema (or STRING in Bronze + typed casts in Silver), and handle genuinely new types through a reviewed change.

debug.title: Bronze doubled after re-running a plain batch load
debug.symptom: Row count in `ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw` jumped to exactly 2× (or 3×) after someone re-ran the ingestion notebook. Same order_ids appear several times, with different `_ingested_at`.
askYourself: Was this load a plain `spark.read` + `mode("append")` with no file tracking?
Did the run read files that a previous run already loaded (same `_source_file` twice)?
Was the job retried or re-run manually?
Can I delete the duplicate load cleanly (by `_ingested_at` / Delta version)?
Should this load be COPY INTO or Auto Loader instead?

steps.do: Count rows per source file and ingestion time.
steps.why: Same file with 2+ ingestion times = re-read duplicates.

steps.do: Check DESCRIBE HISTORY for the extra WRITE/append versions.
Remove the duplicate load (RESTORE to the version before, or DELETE by `_ingested_at`).
Replace the loader with COPY INTO or Auto Loader.
steps.why: Tracks loaded files so re-runs are safe.

rootCauses: Manual or automatic re-run of an append job
debug.fix: Clean up the duplicate append, then switch to an idempotent file loader (COPY INTO / Auto Loader).

debug.title: Checkpoint deleted: old files re-ingested
debug.symptom: After a 'cleanup' or redeploy, Bronze row count jumps. Old files' rows appear again with today's `_ingested_at`; downstream sees duplicates.
askYourself: Is the checkpoint location the same as before — and does it still contain data?
Who or what deleted/reset it (cleanup job, redeploy, path change)?
Which `_source_file`s were ingested twice, and in which Delta versions?
Do I have a copy of the old checkpoint to restore?
If not: reconcile by source file, dedupe downstream, or restart with includeExistingFiles=false?

steps.do: Compare the configured checkpointLocation with the last good run and list its contents.
steps.why: Proves a reset vs a different bug.

steps.do: Find files ingested more than once.
Restore the checkpoint copy if one exists; otherwise delete the duplicate load (by `_ingested_at` / RESTORE).
steps.why: Get Bronze back to one copy per file.

steps.do: Protect the checkpoint path (permissions, no cleanup jobs on /system).

rootCauses: Checkpoint path changed in a deploy
Cleanup script treating checkpoints as temp data
debug.fix: Restore or reconcile, then protect checkpoint paths as operational state. If a fresh start is unavoidable, decide explicitly between re-ingest+dedupe and includeExistingFiles=false.
debug.mnemonic: WHERE → WHO → WHICH FILES → RESTORE or RECONCILE → PROTECT

debug.title: Two streams share one checkpoint
debug.symptom: Two pipelines behave strangely at the same time: one skips files, the other reprocesses or fails with checkpoint/offset errors. Their configs both say `checkpointLocation=/shared/checkpoint`.
askYourself: Which queries write to this checkpoint path?
Did they start sharing it after a copy-paste or a refactor of a common config?
Which files did each stream skip or reprocess?
Can each query get its own fresh checkpoint without losing or duplicating data?

steps.do: Grep job/pipeline configs for the checkpoint path.
Stop both queries.
Give each query a unique checkpoint path derived from its target.
Reconcile missing/duplicate files per target using `_source_file`.
steps.why: Fix the data the confusion caused.

rootCauses: Misunderstanding checkpoint as a generic folder
debug.fix: One checkpoint per streaming query, named after its target; reconcile both targets after the split.

debug.title: Source path changed, checkpoint kept
debug.symptom: After changing `.load("/orders/sourceA")` to `.load("/orders/sourceB")` the stream fails, ingests nothing, or ingests an unexpected mix of files.
askYourself: Did the source path (or query shape) change while the checkpoint stayed the same?
What does the checkpoint believe the source is?
Should sourceB start from scratch (backfill) or only new files?
Will sourceA's data still be needed in the same target?

steps.do: Diff the stream definition against the last good deploy.
Create a new checkpoint (and schemaLocation if needed) for the new source.
steps.why: The old checkpoint describes another query.

steps.do: Decide backfill: includeExistingFiles=true (default) to load sourceB history, or false for only new files.
Verify counts per `_source_file` prefix in the target.

rootCauses: Checkpoint treated as a generic cache
Path change in config without state plan
debug.fix: New source/topology → new checkpoint + explicit backfill decision.

debug.title: Auto Loader table has every column as STRING
debug.symptom: The new Bronze table from Auto Loader shows `order_id STRING, amount STRING, order_ts STRING`; a downstream sum fails or sorts '100' before '20'.
askYourself: Is the source a text format (JSON/CSV/XML) where Auto Loader defaults to STRING?
Did I set `cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes` — and before the schema was first persisted?
Do I actually want strings in Bronze (preserve source) and types in Silver?
Which few columns really need types early — would schema hints do?
Is a full explicit schema justified because the upstream contract is known?

steps.do: Check the schema stored under schemaLocation (`_schemas`) and the table schema.
Decide the layer for typing: Bronze strings + Silver casts is often the safest.
If types are needed at ingestion: add schemaHints for key columns or inferColumnTypes for a new stream.
Cast in Silver with validation.
steps.why: Bad values become quarantinable instead of breaking ingestion.
steps.code: SELECT CAST(order_id AS BIGINT) AS order_id, TRY_CAST(amount AS DOUBLE) AS amount FROM ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw

rootCauses: Default string inference for text formats (by design)
inferColumnTypes not set (or set after schema persisted)
debug.fix: Not a bug: keep strings in Bronze and cast in Silver, or use hints / inferColumnTypes / explicit schema deliberately.
debug.mnemonic: TEXT → STRING; decide WHERE to type

debug.title: Stream stopped right after a new column appeared
debug.symptom: The Auto Loader job failed with an error saying a new field/column was detected (schema change). It worked for weeks. Upstream says they 'added a small field'.
askYourself: Is this the documented addNewColumns behavior (stop, record, restart) rather than a real bug?
Which file introduced the new column — and is the change intentional?
Did the schema in schemaLocation get a new version with the column?
Should this feed evolve, rescue, or fail loudly (schemaEvolutionMode)?
Does the job have retries so a restart picks up the evolved schema?

steps.do: Read the failure message and the latest schema version under schemaLocation/_schemas.
Find the file with the new column (`_metadata.file_path` / landing-zone timestamps).
steps.why: Ties the change to a delivery.

steps.do: Confirm with upstream that the column is intended.
Restart (or rely on job retries); verify the column appears.
steps.why: addNewColumns continues with the new schema after restart.

steps.do: Set schemaEvolutionMode deliberately for this feed.
steps.why: rescue / failOnNewColumns if evolution should not be automatic.

debug.fix: Treat the stop as a control point: confirm intent, restart (job retries), and choose an evolution mode per feed.
debug.mnemonic: STOP → SCHEMA → FILE → OWNER → RESTART → MODE

debug.title: New files exist but no rows appear
debug.symptom: Upstream says files were delivered; the landing zone listing shows them; `ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw` has no new rows. The stream/job shows no errors.
askYourself: Do the new files actually exist where I think?
Does the stream's load path exactly match the landing path?
Are the extension and format what the reader expects?
Did Auto Loader discover them at all (query progress)?
Does the checkpoint say they were already processed (same names)?
Did parsing fail (nulls / `_rescued_data` / corrupt records)?
Is the stream stopped on a schema change?
Did the write to the sink fail?

steps.do: List the landing path and compare with the stream's `.load()` path.
Check format/extension vs `cloudFiles.format` and any filters.
steps.why: A `.csv.gz` or `.JSON` may not be what you expect.

steps.do: Inspect the query's recent progress (input rows, files).
Compare the new file names with already-ingested `_source_file`s.
Query `_rescued_data` / nulls for the latest ingestion.
Check the stream status/errors and the sink table.
steps.why: Schema stops and sink failures end the chain.

debug.fix: Find the first breakpoint along source → sink and fix exactly there (path, format, naming, parser options, schema policy or sink).
debug.mnemonic: EXIST · PATH · FORMAT · FOUND · DONE? · PARSE · SCHEMA · SINK

debug.title: Source file overwritten: the correction never arrived
debug.symptom: Upstream fixed wrong amounts by re-uploading `orders_0928.csv` under the same name. Bronze/Silver still show the old wrong amounts. COPY INTO runs succeed.
askYourself: Was the correction delivered as a NEW file or by overwriting an already-loaded one?
Does COPY INTO / Auto Loader consider that file identity already processed?
Do Bronze rows from that file show the old `_ingested_at` only?
Do I need a deliberate reload (FILES + force) and cleanup of the old rows?
Can upstream switch to immutable, uniquely named deliveries?

steps.do: Compare the file's modification time with the Bronze `_ingested_at` for that `_source_file`.
steps.why: Modified after ingestion = overwritten in place.

steps.do: Confirm the loader skipped it (no new rows for that file).
steps.why: COPY INTO skips loaded files even if changed.

steps.do: Delete the old rows of that file, then reload deliberately.
steps.why: Avoid duplicates while getting the correction in.
steps.code:
DELETE FROM ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw WHERE _source_file LIKE '%orders_0928.csv';

COPY INTO ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw
FROM '/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/orders_csv/'
FILEFORMAT = CSV
FILES = ('orders_0928.csv')
FORMAT_OPTIONS ('header' = 'true')
COPY_OPTIONS ('force' = 'true');

steps.do: Agree on immutable delivery (corrections as new files).

rootCauses: Loader tracks file identity, not content
debug.fix: Reload deliberately (cleanup + FILES + force) and move upstream to immutable, uniquely named files.
debug.mnemonic: SAME NAME = SAME FILE (to the loader)

debug.title: Source schema suddenly changed (STRING → STRUCT)
debug.symptom: Bronze worked yesterday with `amount STRING`; today Auto Loader stops, rescues lots of values, or `amount` contains JSON blobs like `{"value":19.5,"currency":"EUR"}`.
askYourself: Was the source contract intentionally changed?
Did only one corrupt file do this, or every new file?
Should the field be rescued (keep running, inspect later)?
Should the schema evolve (intentional, agreed change)?
Should the stream fail (contract violation that needs review)?

steps.do: Find which files carry the new shape (`_source_file`, `_rescued_data`).
steps.why: One file = bad delivery; all files = contract change.

steps.do: Ask upstream whether the change is intentional and documented.
Choose: rescue (schemaEvolutionMode rescue / rescued column), evolve deliberately, or fail.
Adapt Silver parsing (e.g. extract `amount.value`) only after the decision.
steps.why: Keeps Silver correct across old and new shapes.

debug.fix: Establish intent and scope, then deliberately rescue, evolve or fail; never 'enable everything'.
debug.mnemonic: INTENT → ONE FILE? → RESCUE / EVOLVE / FAIL

debug.title: New upstream column missing from Bronze
debug.symptom: Upstream added `discount` last week. Bronze `orders_raw` has no `discount` column; nothing failed.
askYourself: Which schemaEvolutionMode is in effect (explicit default none? rescue?)
What does the latest schema under schemaLocation contain?
Am I providing a strict explicit schema that doesn't list `discount`?
Is the value sitting in `_rescued_data` — and is rescue even enabled?
Did the stream actually restart after an addNewColumns stop?

steps.do: Read the stream definition: `.schema(...)`, schemaEvolutionMode, rescuedDataColumn.
steps.why: Explicit schema → mode none → column ignored.

steps.do: Inspect the latest schema version in schemaLocation.
steps.why: With inference + addNewColumns the new column should appear there.

steps.do: Query `_rescued_data` for `discount`.
steps.why: In rescue mode (or with rescuedDataColumn) the values are preserved.
steps.code: SELECT _rescued_data FROM ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw WHERE _rescued_data LIKE '%discount%' LIMIT 10;

steps.do: If the column is wanted: add it to the explicit schema / switch mode, and backfill from rescued data or source files.
steps.why: Deliberate evolution plus recovery of the missed values.

rootCauses: Stream not restarted after evolution stop
debug.fix: Check mode → schemaLocation → explicit schema → rescued data; then evolve deliberately and backfill.

debug.title: Duplicated business IDs in Bronze/Silver
debug.symptom: `order_id = 100` appears twice (or more) in Bronze and/or Silver.
askYourself: Was the same source file loaded twice?
Do two different files both contain the ID?
Was it an upstream retry/resend?
Is the Silver MERGE/dedup missing or keyed wrongly?
Was a checkpoint reset (or COPY INTO forced)?

steps.do: Group the duplicates by `_source_file` and `_ingested_at`.
steps.why: Same file twice = ingestion; different files = source.

steps.do: If same file twice: look for checkpoint resets, force reloads, plain re-reads.
If different files: confirm with upstream (retry/resend/update).
Check the Silver MERGE: dedupe source by key, match on business key only.

rootCauses: Same file ingested twice (checkpoint reset / force / re-read)
debug.fix: Separate file idempotency (fix loads/state) from business-key idempotency (dedupe/MERGE in Silver). Don't immediately blame Auto Loader.
debug.mnemonic: SAME FILE? · OTHER FILE? · RETRY? · MERGE? · RESET?

debug.title: Malformed CSV rows
debug.symptom: A CSV feed produces parse errors, rows with null amounts, values in `_rescued_data`/`_corrupt_record`, or rows with unexpected extra columns — e.g. a line `2,"10.5`.
askYourself: What does the raw line look like around the failure?
Is the quote character right — and is there an unclosed quote?
How are quotes escaped inside fields (escape)?
Do quoted fields contain newlines (multiLine)?
Is the delimiter right, and is the header option correct?
Which mode is hiding or surfacing the bad rows?

steps.do: Read the raw text of the file to see the exact bad line.
steps.why: You need the real grammar, not a guess.

steps.do: Compare quote/escape/multiLine/delimiter/header with the file.
Make bad rows visible: PERMISSIVE + columnNameOfCorruptRecord (or rescued data).
Fix options or get upstream to fix the export; quarantine the bad rows.
steps.why: Clean data continues; bad data stays inspectable.

debug.fix: Look at the raw line, align quote/escape/multiLine/delimiter/header with the file, keep bad rows visible and quarantined.
debug.mnemonic: RAW → QUOTE → ESCAPE → MULTILINE → DELIM/HEADER → MODE

pitfalls.title: No header option → header becomes data
pitfalls.text: Reading a CSV with a header line but without `.option("header","true")` gives columns `_c0, _c1…` AND an extra data row containing the column names — which later fails every cast.
pitfalls.fix: Always state `header` explicitly for CSV (and check the first rows with display()).

pitfalls.title: CSV without schema = all STRING
pitfalls.text: Plain CSV has no native types. With neither `.schema(...)` nor `inferSchema=true`, every CSV column is read as **STRING**.
pitfalls.fix: Pass an explicit schema (production) or set inferSchema for exploration.

pitfalls.title: Inference is a moving target
pitfalls.text: Monday's files make Spark infer `amount INT`; Tuesday's file has `100.50` → the inferred type changes (or parsing breaks). Downstream writes then hit schema mismatches.
pitfalls.fix: Have a deliberate schema policy: explicit schema (or Auto Loader with schemaLocation + hints) for production ingestion.

pitfalls.title: STREAM read_files = Auto Loader underneath
pitfalls.text: When `read_files` is used with `STREAM` in a streaming table, Databricks runs **Auto Loader** for incremental file ingestion. Everything you learn about Auto Loader (checkpoints, schema inference, rescued data) applies.
pitfalls.fix: Treat `STREAM read_files(...)` as the SQL face of Auto Loader.

pitfalls.title: _metadata isn't in SELECT *
pitfalls.text: The `_metadata` column is hidden: `select("*")` or `SELECT *` won't return it, so audit columns silently go missing.
pitfalls.fix: Select `_metadata` (or `_metadata.file_path`) explicitly and alias it, e.g. `_source_file`.

pitfalls.title: Date-folder filtering is fragile incremental logic
pitfalls.text: Filtering by filename/date assumes a perfect upstream layout. Late files, backfills, re-uploads, timezone bugs, renames and missing folders all cause skipped or duplicated data.
pitfalls.fix: Use a tool that tracks processed files: COPY INTO or Auto Loader.

pitfalls.title: A changed file is still 'already loaded'
pitfalls.text: Databricks: if a file was already loaded, COPY INTO **skips it on later runs even if the file's contents have changed**. Same tracked file identity ≠ 'reload because content changed'.
pitfalls.fix: Deliver corrections as NEW files (immutable delivery). To deliberately reload, use `COPY_OPTIONS ('force' = 'true')` and handle duplicates.

pitfalls.title: PATTERN is a glob, not a regex
pitfalls.text: COPY INTO's PATTERN is a **glob pattern** (`*`, `?`, `[a-z]`, `{a,b}`). The tutoring notes wrote a regex-style `'orders_.*[.]csv'` — as a glob that means 'orders_.' + anything + '.csv' and would NOT match `orders_001.csv`.
pitfalls.fix: Write globs: `PATTERN = 'orders_*.csv'`. Test with VALIDATE or a small run.

pitfalls.title: Two different mergeSchema options
pitfalls.text: `FORMAT_OPTIONS mergeSchema` reconciles schemas across source files; `COPY_OPTIONS mergeSchema` evolves the target Delta schema. Setting only one may not give you new columns in the table.
pitfalls.fix: Remember: FORMAT = files being read, COPY = target being written.

pitfalls.title: Auto Loader is not 'faster spark.read'
pitfalls.text: Auto Loader doesn't read an individual file faster. Its value is incremental file discovery, remembered state, schema handling and streaming integration.
pitfalls.fix: Answer 'why Auto Loader?' with discovery + state + schema + streaming, not raw speed.

pitfalls.title: schemaLocation ≠ progress
pitfalls.text: `cloudFiles.schemaLocation` stores **schema history/state**, not stream progress. Progress lives in the **checkpoint**. Exam questions swap them on purpose.
pitfalls.fix: Shape → schemaLocation. Progress → checkpointLocation.

pitfalls.title: Checkpoint on ephemeral disk
pitfalls.text: `checkpointLocation="/tmp/checkpoint"` lives on a worker's local disk. When the cluster terminates, the checkpoint vanishes → the stream loses all progress.
pitfalls.fix: Put checkpoints on persistent storage: a Unity Catalog Volume or cloud path, e.g. `/Volumes/ecommerce/system/orders_checkpoint/`.

pitfalls.title: Checkpoint = operational state
pitfalls.text: Deleting, resetting or moving a checkpoint wipes the stream's memory of what it processed. Re-ingestion and duplicates follow.
pitfalls.fix: Never treat checkpoints as disposable temp data. Back them up/protect them; reset only deliberately, with a reconciliation plan.

pitfalls.title: Shared checkpoint path
pitfalls.text: Two unrelated streaming queries writing to the same checkpoint location can corrupt each other's progress and state: one may skip files, the other reprocess, or the stream fails.
pitfalls.fix: One checkpoint location per streaming query — derive it from the target name, e.g. `/Volumes/<cat>/system/<table>_checkpoint/`.

pitfalls.title: Changed source, same checkpoint
pitfalls.text: Keeping a checkpoint after changing the source path (or other topology) mixes the old query's progress with a new input: files can be skipped, re-read or the stream can fail.
pitfalls.fix: New source/topology → new checkpoint, plus an explicit backfill/reconciliation plan.

pitfalls.title: Auto Loader defaults text formats to STRING
pitfalls.text: Unlike `spark.read` with inferSchema, Auto Loader infers JSON/CSV/XML columns as STRING unless `cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes=true`.
pitfalls.fix: Expect strings in Bronze; use inferColumnTypes, schema hints or Silver casts when you need types.

pitfalls.title: Inferred once, remembered after
pitfalls.text: Inference runs when the stream first builds its schema and the result is persisted in schemaLocation. Flipping `inferColumnTypes` later on an existing stream doesn't magically re-infer the stored schema.
pitfalls.fix: Decide inference options before the first run; for an existing stream use schema hints or Silver casts (or a deliberately new stream with a new schemaLocation/checkpoint).

pitfalls.title: A failing stream after a new column isn't (necessarily) a bug
pitfalls.text: With the default addNewColumns mode, the first batch that contains a new column stops the stream after recording the new schema. Restarting picks it up.
pitfalls.fix: Run Auto Loader as a Job with retries; decide per feed whether new columns should evolve, be rescued, or fail loudly.

pitfalls.title: Explicit schema hides new columns
pitfalls.text: With a strict explicit schema the evolution mode defaults to `none`: a new upstream column does NOT appear as a regular column and isn't rescued unless you set `rescuedDataColumn`.
pitfalls.fix: Add `.option("rescuedDataColumn", "_rescued_data")` and monitor it, or change the schema deliberately.

pitfalls.title: Exactly-once ≠ no duplicate keys
pitfalls.text: Exactly-once file ingestion guarantees each *file* is ingested once. Two distinct files (an upstream retry, a resend, an update) can legitimately contain the same order_id.
pitfalls.fix: Deduplicate / MERGE on the business key in Silver (or the CDC layer).

pitfalls.title: Transforming (and dropping) during ingestion
pitfalls.text: Bronze that applies business rules, joins and drops malformed rows loses the raw evidence; when a rule is wrong you can't rebuild.
pitfalls.fix: Ingestion ≠ transformation: keep Bronze conservative, do business logic in Silver/Gold.

pitfalls.title: Millions of files arriving continuously
pitfalls.text: Exam: 'millions of files arriving continuously in cloud object storage — which mechanism?' Answer: **Auto Loader** — not repeated spark.read, and typically not COPY INTO at that scale.
pitfalls.fix: Scale + continuous arrivals → Auto Loader.

pitfalls.title: Overwriting source files in place
pitfalls.text: Incremental loaders reason about **file identity**. An overwritten file may be skipped as 'already loaded' (lost correction) or, with overwrites allowed, reprocessed (duplicates).
pitfalls.fix: Agree on immutable landing zones: unique file names, corrections as new files.

pitfalls.title: Don't blindly allow everything
pitfalls.text: Turning on every evolution option lets an accidental upstream change (e.g. amount becoming a struct) flow silently into Silver and Gold.
pitfalls.fix: Decide per change: evolve (intentional), rescue (unexpected but keep), or fail (contract violation).

pitfalls.title: multiLine + broken quote = swallowed rows
pitfalls.text: With `multiLine=true`, an unclosed quote can make the parser treat the following lines as part of one field — several good rows can vanish into one bad record.
pitfalls.fix: Inspect raw lines around the failure, fix quote/escape settings, and keep corrupt/rescued records visible instead of dropping them.

flashcards.a: Bringing data that lives outside the platform into it — here, files into Delta tables.

flashcards.q: Six questions every ingestion pipeline answers?
flashcards.a: Where is the data → discover → read → interpret with schema → remember what's processed → write reliably to Delta.
Batch: reads the path's current contents, no memory of earlier runs.

flashcards.q: CSV without the header option gives which column names?
flashcards.a: `_c0, _c1, _c2…` — and the header line becomes a data row.
`.option("delimiter", "|")` (alias `sep`).
PERMISSIVE (default, nulls + optional corrupt column), DROPMALFORMED (drop), FAILFAST (throw).

flashcards.q: CSV with no schema and no inferSchema → column types?
flashcards.a: All STRING.

flashcards.q: Why does schema inference cost time?
flashcards.a: Spark must inspect the data to decide types before the real read (extra pass).

flashcards.q: Two ways to pass an explicit schema?
flashcards.a: A StructType of StructFields, or a DDL string like `"order_id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE"`.

flashcards.q: Five benefits of explicit schema in production?
flashcards.a: Faster (no inference pass), predictable, version-controlled, no type surprises, easier validation.
Monday amounts 100, 200 → INT; Tuesday 100.50 → DOUBLE: the inferred type changes between runs.

flashcards.q: What does a nested JSON object become?
flashcards.a: A struct column (e.g. `customer.name`).
Its schema (names + types) is stored in the file.

flashcards.q: CSV vs JSON vs Parquet in one line each?
